label: Combinatorial Description
notes: Open the lecture. Vassiliev invariants admit a purely combinatorial description in terms of diagrams and algebras of graphs. The lecture assembles the algebra of chord diagrams, the role of the four-term relation, the Hopf algebra structure, and how Lie algebras produce explicit weight systems.

label: The Algebra of Diagrams
notes: Form a vector space spanned by chord diagrams of each degree and impose the four-term relation. Connected sum of diagrams along the circle makes this a graded algebra. Its dual is the space of weight systems, so understanding the algebra of diagrams is equivalent to understanding all top-order Vassiliev symbols at once.

label: From Chords to Trivalent Graphs
notes: Enlarge chord diagrams to allow internal trivalent vertices, giving the larger space of closed diagrams. The four-term relation becomes the STU relation, and antisymmetry and the Jacobi-like IHX relation govern the internal vertices. This graph algebra is more flexible and reveals hidden structure invisible at the chord level.

label: The Hopf Algebra Structure
notes: Equip the diagram algebra with a coproduct that splits a diagram into pairs of subdiagrams. With the connected-sum product this makes a graded connected Hopf algebra. By a structure theorem it is freely generated by its primitive elements, drastically reducing the data needed to describe invariants of every order.

label: Lie Algebra Weight Systems
notes: Construct concrete weight systems from a Lie algebra with an invariant bilinear form: assign structure constants to trivalent vertices and the form to chords, then contract. The IHX relation reflects the Jacobi identity, so the construction is consistent. These weight systems recover the coefficients of the classical quantum invariants.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. The combinatorial side of Vassiliev theory lives in a Hopf algebra of trivalent graph diagrams modulo STU, IHX, and antisymmetry, dual to weight systems. Lie algebras feed in concrete examples. The next lecture builds the Kontsevich integral, the analytic bridge completing the theory.
